claims.text: Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 fabricated by conventional deposition forms Cr–V-rich precipitates at approximately 8 dpa.
High-energy mechanical alloying followed by short-duration, high-temperature spark plasma sintering can fabricate W38Ta36Cr15V11.
The proposed processing route is practically suitable for bulk manufacture of W38Ta36Cr15V11.
Mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering will improve elemental mixing in W38Ta36Cr15V11.
Mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering will refine the grain structure of W38Ta36Cr15V11.
The processed alloy will have a chemically homogeneous nanocrystalline matrix.
Grain refinement will increase defect-sink density.
The increased defect-sink density and chemical homogeneity will minimize irradiation-induced segregation of Cr and V.
Improved alloying-element dispersion will reduce local Cr and V concentration fluctuations.
Reducing local Cr and V concentration fluctuations will decrease the number of nucleation sites for Cr–V-rich precipitates during irradiation.
The proposed processing route will suppress Cr–V-rich precipitate formation in W38Ta36Cr15V11 at approximately 8 dpa.
Processed specimens will contain minimal or no Cr–V-rich precipitates after irradiation to approximately 8 dpa.
The processed alloy will preserve low irradiation-induced hardening and radiation resistance.
Processed specimens will exhibit a hardness increase comparable to or lower than that of conventionally processed specimens.
The baseline W38Ta36Cr15V11 experiences irradiation hardening at approximately 8 dpa.
The intervention is expected to remain effective at the moderate-to-high specimen temperatures relevant to fusion plasma-facing materials.
The thermal stability of the processed alloy under extended high-temperature service remains uncertain.

contradictions.description: The query characterizes irradiated nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 as showing negligible hardening, whereas the baseline states that it experiences irradiation hardening at approximately 8 dpa.
